extracted.intended_audience: poets, students/scholars of classical literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry and dramatic writing, drawn from Horace's Epistles and accompanying commentary—covering audience, style, editing, adaptation, and moral/social function of verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity before busy patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Burdened as you are, Caesar, with cares of State, you must not be approached by me in a long discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing a powerful or busy patron (or any audience with constrained attention), keep the address concise; do not delay their time with long oration. Tailor length to the listener's circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for readers, not for spectators
rubrics_metrics.description: I pray you, O Caesar, to bestow a share of your patronage on those who write, not for spectators, but for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer literary qualities that endure on the page rather than ephemeral stage spectacle. Value subtlety, craft, and written complexity that rewards reading over theatrical tricks aimed solely at immediate applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate poet for grand subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: If I could sing your exploits I should much prefer to sing your exploits, but you are worthy of a greater poet, and I will not run the risk of bringing discredit upon you as well as upon myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match subject matter and patron to the author's ability; avoid taking on exalted topics unless you possess the mastery to treat them without dishonourably diminishing the subject or yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to vulgar spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The masses call for bears and boxers, and even the educated care more for what delights the restless eye than for good drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on sensationalism or mere stage attractions to win approval. Prioritize artistic integrity over crowd-pleasing spectacles that substitute show for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate between ancient and modern works on merit, not age alone
rubrics_metrics.description: This admiration should be more discriminating, for these early writers are far from perfect... It is really envy of contemporary merit that accounts for this undue praise of the old writers and a depreciation of the new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by their intrinsic qualities rather than simply their age or received reputation; avoid automatic deference to 'ancient' works and be open to contemporary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish, concinnity and decorum in verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter quae verbum emicuit si forte decorum, et si versus paulo concinnior unus et alter, iniuste totum ducit venditque poema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek overall polish and harmonious arrangement; one or two pleasing phrases should not be allowed to carry or excuse a whole poem's defects. Strive for consistent decorum and balanced workmanship across the whole piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise ruthlessly (the art of blotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: He lacks 'the last and greatest art, the art to blot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing—deleting, cutting, and refining—is an essential craft skill. Authors must be willing to remove beloved but faulty material to improve the whole work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy requires more careful labour because indulgence is less
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy... carries a heavier burden, as the indulgence allowed is less... Comedy drawing its themes from daily life calls for less labour; but in truth it carries a heavier burden, as the indulgence allowed is less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing comedy, pay meticulous attention to craft: everyday subjects demand precision, controlled taste, and craftsmanship because audiences grant less leniency for roughness or slackness than for certain lofty tragic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse scurrility and abusive songs (observe social limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with rude Fescennine verses, whose scurrility had to be checked by law... at last a law was carried with a penalty, forbidding the portrayal of any in abusive strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of social and legal boundaries: coarse, abusive, or malicious lampoons—even in festive or rustic forms—can lead to social harm and legal sanction. Wit should not be wantonly cruel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate/adapt from Greek with dignity and worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: He also made essay, whether he could reproduce in worthy style, and took pride in his success... the word vertere means not merely to 'translate' but to 'transfer' from the Greek to the Roman stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation requires more than literal translation; it demands assimilating and re-creating material in the target culture's idiom and aesthetic—only transfer Greek models when you can render them worthy in your own style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow one bright phrase to mask overall faults
rubrics_metrics.description: If among them a pleasing phrase shines forth, or one or two lines are somewhat better turned—then these unfairly carry off and sell the whole poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and creators should guard against overvaluing isolated flashes of brilliance that conceal structural or stylistic weaknesses; judge the whole piece, not just memorable lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's social and moral functions
rubrics_metrics.description: They promote the education of the young and serve the cause of religion... The poet fashions the tender, lisping lips of childhood... He tells of noble deeds, equips the rising age with famous examples, and to the helpless and sick at heart brings comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and cultivate poetry's role in moral instruction, social cohesion, religious ritual, and consolation. Consider the ethical and pedagogic effects of verse as part of its value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of selling craft for profit (avoid mercenary shortcuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus... being more anxious to fill his purse than to write good plays... he is eager to drop a coin into his pocket and, that done, he cares not whether his play fall or stand square on its feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist motivations that prioritize immediate financial gain over artistic quality; shortcuts for profit often produce slipshod, careless work that harms long-term reputation and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste shifts—do not assume permanence of preference
rubrics_metrics.description: What pleases or is hated, what you would not think changeable? Such was the effect of happy times of peace and prosperous gales... what she wanted in impatience, she soon, when satisfied, cast off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for changing public tastes and fashions when composing and when evaluating works; what pleases now may be cast off tomorrow—aim for qualities that can survive fluctuations of taste.
